items.title: Show HN: Armin – Modern Anki alternative with prerrequisite graphs
items.summary: okay, so a bit of context. back when i was studying at college, i was trying to optimize my learning process as much as possible, and i ended up discovering Anki and spaced-repetition as a concept. i ended up using Anki for quite a while and it did help me. i loved the concept... but i didn't like the app. it had me conflicted. on one hand, it allowed me to properly review the content from my classes (among other stuff), but on the other it had way too many quirks and complicated ways of handling things that i wasn't a fan of (in particular, the UX leaves a lot to be desired, although it has marginally improved in recent years). i ended up churning from Anki and just abandoning the practice of spaced repetition altogether. after some time, i ended up reading this article recommended by Justin Skycak https://lelouch.dev/blog/you-are-probably-not-dumb/ . the tldr is that knowledge has prerrequisites, and if you don't have them, you won't fully understand what you are trying to learn in the first place. and that was one of my annoyances with Anki. as i kept reviewing stuff (especially pre-made decks) Anki assumes all knowledge is in the same layer of understanding. it assumes that each flashcard is independent from the others, and that makes it difficult to actually progress while trying to learn a particular topic. Justin Skycak (the guy from Math Academy) ended up implementing spaced-repetition + prerrequisite graphs for math learning, and there i ended up seeing we could extend the concept more generally. one of the things Math Academy made me realize is that if we combine spaced-repetition (i.e. when we should review a card) with prerrequisite graphs (i.e. we keep unlocking new knowledge as we learn the prerrequisites), we can learn things more clearly and in a more structured way. that's where my "bet" goes. i want something like Anki, but with the option to create a graph of prerrequisites (e.g. you can't learn Y until you properly learn X). that's Armin. among other stuff, i also tried to fix some of the annoyances i had with Anki and make it as intuitive as possible to use. this is a non-exhaustive list of the things i worked on for this app: - UI polish of the interface. i tried to make it as intuitive as possible. - MCP server for letting agents read, edit and manage cards and decks. in particular, the MCP server is very useful for creating flashcards from any existing content you have. just point your agent to a resource (e.g. a pdf) and it will take its content and transform it into a deck with flashcards with its prerrequisites graph already created. - Anki-compatibility with caveats. the app supports bringing your existing Anki decks for most decks out there. however, some decks have custom cards that are not so easy to integrate seamlessly. there are plans to support custom cards in the future, but for now they are not implemented. - graph view that shows all your flashcards. in here, you can create a graph of prerrequisites and further structure your decks. - "concept cards". they work more like exercises. you provide the template of an exercise (e.g. how to calculate a derivative) and an agent creates variations of that same type of exercise while changing the details (like the values). we also have a paid plan for creating way more flashcards and use "concept" cards, but i built the free plan with generous limits so you can test the app without any issue. to be honest, i want the app to be as flexible as possible, and most people will probably only need the free plan. but hey, if you find it too tight, please hit me up and i'll see how i can improve the experience for everyone. the app is open source and MIT-licensed. you can find it here https://github.com/andy-spike/armin as for the rest, it is the same you would expect from a spaced-repetition flashcard app. please try it out and tell me what you think of it!

items.title: Claude Code's API billing depends on how often the cache expires
items.summary: Hello, HN! I’m Max, CTO at Hystax. We use Claude a lot in our development work, and we’re also trying to make coding agents cheaper to run. We built the open-source Kompressor for compressing identical tool outputs that agents constantly resend. In our Codex tests, we noticed a real cost reduction of 22.7%. But testing it with Claude Code, we found something completely different. In Claude Code, the cache plays a more crucial role than compression. Claude Code marks its messages with caching points. As a result, almost every request consists of a long cached prefix and a new, truncated final part. Based on practical experience with Opus 5.5, reading from the cache appears to cost $0.20 per million tokens, accounting for about 92–95% of the tokens charged for prompts. Meanwhile, a five-minute cache entry costs $5, which is 25 times more expensive than reading from the cache. When an agent needs to run a build or a longer training cycle, they face the problem of the cache expiring. The next request then has to write the prefix to the cache again. We saw this 33 times in a cycle of 89-task runs without compression. As a result, 927,000 tokens were rewritten, which is approximately one-third of the volume billed in full. Until now, we’ve deliberately left the Claude Code text uncompressed because overwriting any byte within a cached prefix would very likely cause it to become invalid. But here’s what we came up with instead: – Compress only the uncached part. On the first transmission, only the new part is compressed. Everything already cached stays byte-for-byte unchanged. Fragments shorter than 4,000 characters are sent in full, since compressing each fragment would be much more expensive than sending the entire dialogue as is. – Keep the cache active while the tools are running; don’t let it expire. While the agent waits for a tool response (model building/training), Kompressor resends the last request every 4.5 minutes with max_tokens: 1, so Anthropic re-reads the cached dialogue, and the five-minute timer restarts. Pings stop on the agent’s next request, after ~50 min, on the first failed attempt, or if a ping finds nothing in the cache. – Switch to the one-hour cache only when necessary. After the first pause longer than 5 min, Kompressor requests a one-hour cache for that conversation. We ran Claude Code on the Opus 5.5 model through the Terminal-Bench 2.1 benchmark (89 tasks) and calculated the cost based on Anthropic's actual billing, including pings. The cost per run decreased from $35.35 to $28.30 (-20%). The percentage of tasks solved by the agent without compression was 89.9%, and 90.6% when using Kompressor. The number of tokens lost due to cache expiration decreased from 927,000 to 13,000. But there’s a caveat: the agent never solves the same task twice in exactly the same way, and the entire difference came down to just 4 out of the 89 tasks. We expect these savings to persist from run to run: about 11% from keeping the cache up to date, and a few more percentage points from compression. This effect is most noticeable on tasks where the agent waits a long time – more than five minutes – for a command to execute: model training, compilation, and long simulations. In those cases, costs decreased by 34%. To try Kompressor, see the GitHub repo below. Setup is in the README. The default configuration already includes compression of new text only and a switch to an hourly cache on long pauses; “keep-warm” is off (the only request that the proxy sends on its own). To enable, add to your config: [proxy.providers.anthropic] cache_keep_warm = true and then run: kompressor wrap claude The benchmark above was run with all these settings enabled. Here are cost calculations: https://optscale.ai/blog/claude-code-prompt-caching If you run long tasks in Claude Code, how often does the cache expire while a tool is still running? Have you seen this with other providers too?
